title: From stimulus to spike
objective: Trace how a physical stimulus becomes action potentials travelling to the spinal cord.

steps.title: Every sense does the same three things
steps.body:
A sensory neuron has one job: turn something physical into the brain's currency, electrical spikes.

1. **[[transduction|Transduction]]:** a stimulus (force, heat, a chemical) opens ion channels in the nerve ending.
2. **[[receptor potential|Receptor potential]]:** ions flow and the ending depolarizes. The bigger the stimulus, the bigger this graded change.
3. **Encoding:** if the receptor potential crosses [[threshold]], the neuron fires [[action potential|action potentials]] that travel to the CNS.

steps.prompt: Put the steps in order for a [[DRG]] neuron sensing a pinch.
items: Cations flow in; receptor potential builds
steps.explanation: Stimulus → channel → graded receptor potential → threshold → all-or-none spikes → CNS. The same chain works for heat or chemicals; only the channel at the start changes.

steps.title: Each neuron has a favorite stimulus
steps.body:
Each sensory neuron responds best to one kind of energy, its **[[adequate stimulus]]**. Touch neurons respond to gentle force, cold neurons to cooling, [[nociceptor|nociceptors]] to stimuli intense enough to threaten damage.

The channels a neuron expresses largely set its favorite stimulus. That's why A3 (TRP channels) and A4 (Piezo channels) matter so much.

steps.prompt: Why does a touch neuron ignore a warm surface?
options: Warmth opens its channels, but the brain filters out signals from touch fibers
It lacks heat-gated channels, so warming opens nothing in its ending
Its myelin sheath insulates the nerve ending from the surrounding warmth
Heat closes its sodium channels, so it transduces but can never spike
steps.explanation: Selectivity starts at transduction. Without a heat-gated channel, warmth produces no receptor potential, so nothing gets encoded.

variants.setup: The skin above a pure touch (Aβ) ending is gently warmed by a heat lamp (warm, not hot). Nothing touches or moves the skin.
options: Fires briskly, treating the warmth as a strong stimulus
Stays silent; it has no heat-gated channels to open
Fires a single spike and then adapts to the warmth
Depolarizes slowly but never reaches its threshold
variants.reveal: Selectivity is set at transduction: no heat channel, no receptor potential, no firing. (Pressing on that skin *would* fire it — but that's force, not heat.)

steps.setup: A drug blocks voltage-gated sodium channels along the axon but leaves the channels in the nerve ending alone. You press on the skin.
options: No receptor potential forms, since the ending can no longer depolarize
A receptor potential still forms, but no spikes travel to the spinal cord
Spikes reach the cord normally, because transduction is left untouched
The ending fires continuously, since blocking Nav removes a brake
steps.reveal: Transduction still works, so the ending depolarizes. Without sodium channels, though, no action potential can be generated or conducted, so the CNS hears nothing. This is how local anesthetics like lidocaine work.

variants.prompt: Lidocaine blocks the voltage-gated Na⁺ channels along a sensory axon. You pinch the skin, but nothing is felt. Why?
options: No receptor potential forms, since the ending can no longer depolarize
A receptor potential still forms, but no spikes travel to the spinal cord
Spikes reach the cord normally, because transduction is left untouched
The ending fires continuously, since blocking Nav removes a brake
variants.explanation: Transduction (the receptor potential) is intact; with Nav blocked, no action potential forms or propagates, so the CNS hears nothing.
